etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English mornen, mournen, from Old English murnan, from Proto-Germanic *murnaną. Cognate with French morne (“gloomy”).

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To express sadness or sorrow for; to grieve over (especially a death).

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Sixt”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: We mourn in black; why mourn we not in blood?

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Genesis 23:2:
quote.text: Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.

quote.citation: 2012, BioWare, Mass Effect 3 (Science Fiction), Redwood City: Electronic Arts, →OCLC, PC, scene: Nightmare:
quote.text: Thane Krios: It seems there will be no one to mourn me when I die. You're the only friend I've made in ten years.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To utter in a sorrowful manner.

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, “vij”, in Le Morte Darthur, book II:
quote.text: Anone after ther cam balen / and whan he sawe kynge Arthur / he alyght of his hors / and cam to the kynge on foote / and salewed hym / by my hede saide Arthur ye be welcome / Sire ryght now cam rydynge this way a knyght makynge grete moorne / for what cause I can not telle(please add an English translation of this quotation)
